entries.clue: Most modest, I agree to get into bed (6)

indicatorNotes.to get into: Getting into something means ending up inside it, so the words of assent are placed within the other piece.

blocks.note: a cot is a bed, the child's one, and it opens up to take the rest
'I agree' spoken aloud is yes, three letters going straight in

annotation.surface: Someone agreeable is being invited to climb into bed.
annotation.walkthrough: 'I agree' is a whole phrase standing in for a single word of assent, which is unusual enough to look like padding. The bed is the nursery kind, three letters long.
annotation.definitionFit: Coy means shyly modest, and the superlative of it is what the superlative definition asks for.

entries.clue: Miner’s dog runs (7)

blocks.note: the collie is the sheepdog breed, six letters taken whole
R is how a cricket scorebook writes runs

annotation.surface: A miner's dog goes for a run.
annotation.walkthrough: The possessive 's is doing the work of 'is', holding the definition against the wordplay and contributing nothing itself. Cricket's scorecard is where the single letter for runs comes from.
annotation.definitionFit: A collier is a coal miner, the word still heard in the old pit villages, and also the ship that carried the coal.

entries.clue: 12 months with Braverman, ultimately, is long (5)

indicatorNotes.ultimately: Ultimately means at the very end of things, so only the final letter of the name beside it is taken.

blocks.note: twelve months make a year
Suella Braverman is a Conservative MP and former home secretary; her surname ends on N

annotation.surface: A year in Braverman's company is a long one.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Long' closes the clue as the verb, to long for something, and the surface dresses it as the adjective describing the year. Only the final letter of the politician is wanted.
annotation.definitionFit: To yearn for something is to long for it — the same ache of wanting, and the same part of speech.

entries.clue: That woman will account for gramophone record (7)

blocks.note: that woman is she, the pronoun pointing at her
will contracts to 'll, as in she'll, and the two letters follow the pronoun
ac is the standard short form of account, as on a bank statement

annotation.surface: A woman offers to settle the bill for an old record.
annotation.walkthrough: The contraction is the trick worth filing away: a pronoun and 'will' run together into three letters that no abbreviation list will tell you about. 78rpm discs were pressed from resin, which is why the material can name the disc.
annotation.definitionFit: Old gramophone records were made of shellac, and the word for the resin came to stand for the discs themselves.

entries.clue: One goes up for flowers (6)

blocks.note: one is I in Roman numerals
whatever goes up rises, the verb swapped in whole and in the same tense

annotation.surface: Somebody gets to their feet to fetch flowers.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Goes up' looks like an instruction to turn a word round and is a plain synonym to be swapped in instead. Flowers is doing honest duty here rather than the setter's usual river trick.
annotation.definitionFit: Irises are the tall bearded garden flowers, and the plural definition matches the plural answer.

entries.clue: Resumption of relaxation with paintings, perhaps (7)

indicatorNotes.perhaps: Perhaps admits the word beside it is only one instance of something wider, so the general word for the class is what goes in.

blocks.note: relaxation is rest, four letters taken whole
paintings are one kind of art, which is the broader word wanted

annotation.surface: Time off spent among paintings.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' is the setter signalling a for-instance: paintings are art, but art is not only paintings, so the wider word is the one to write. Both halves are nouns, as the definition is.
annotation.definitionFit: A restart is the resumption of something that had stopped, the noun for taking it up again.

entries.clue: Fish is rock singer with a low voice (5,4)

blocks.note: a rock is a stone, the noun swapped for its synonym
the lowest male singing voice is the bass

annotation.surface: A deep-voiced rock singer is introduced.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Rock singer' wants to be read as one job description and splits down the middle into two unrelated words. The second half is also a fish in its own right, which is half the answer's charm.
annotation.definitionFit: The stone bass is a real sea fish, the wreckfish that shelters round sunken wrecks in warm Atlantic water.

entries.clue: Respect supply staff (7)

indicatorNotes.supply: Read as the adverb of supple — SUPP-lee — it means in a bending, limber way, and letters that bend do not keep their order.

blocks.note: seven letters for the pile, taken for their spelling rather than their meaning

annotation.surface: Respect is due to the people who supply the staff.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Supply' is the crossword's favourite two-faced word: not the verb to provide but the adverb from supple, said with the stress on the front. The staff wanted is a rod, not a workforce.
annotation.definitionFit: A sceptre is the ornamental staff a monarch carries at a coronation, so 'staff' is the pole sense of the word.

entries.clue: Almost alongside (4,2)

blocks.note: the 'very nearly' reading, the one that turns up in set phrases about having almost none of something
the plain spatial reading, one thing set beside another

annotation.surface: Something has not quite pulled level with the thing beside it.
annotation.walkthrough: Two words of clue and no wordplay at all, so each word has to be a definition on its own. The first sense lives almost entirely inside set phrases.
annotation.definitionFit: Next to means beside in the plain spatial sense, and in phrases like 'next to nothing' or 'next to impossible' it means very nearly.

entries.clue: Senior don peels orange, I suspect (3-3,9)

indicatorNotes.suspect: Something you suspect cannot be trusted to be what it presents itself as, and letters under suspicion will not stay in the order handed over.

blocks.note: fifteen letters for the pile; the comma is punctuation for the surface only

annotation.surface: An elderly academic peels an orange, and the speaker is not sure about him.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Peels' looks exactly like an instruction to strip a word's outer letters, and it is fodder — every word from 'don' to the comma goes into the pile. The enumeration's hyphen comes after the first three letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A senior, in the sense of someone past retirement age, is the person drawing the state pension.

entries.clue: Intimate snuggling is generally nice after lunch, first of all (6)

indicatorNotes.first of all: Taking things first of all means starting at the front of each one, so only the opening letter of every word in the run is used.

blocks.clueFragment: snuggling is generally nice after lunch
blocks.note: the six words give up their opening letters in the order they stand

annotation.surface: Close cuddling is usually at its best straight after lunch.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Intimate' is the verb meaning to hint at something, stressed on the last syllable, not the cosy adjective the rest of the sentence dresses it as. The instruction sits at the end and looks back over the six words in front of it.
annotation.definitionFit: To intimate something is to make it known indirectly, which is what you do when you signal it rather than say it.

entries.clue: Item of underwear found in drinks carrier, leading to mockery (8)

indicatorNotes.found in: A thing found in another is sitting inside it, so the garment's letters go within the letters of what carries the drinks.

blocks.note: drinks are carried round on a tray, which then opens after its third letter
in Britain a vest is the undershirt worn next to the skin

annotation.surface: Underwear turns up on the drinks tray, to general derision.
annotation.walkthrough: The British vest is the undershirt, not the American waistcoat, which is what makes it underwear at all. The word wanted is the one in 'a travesty of justice' — an imitation so bad it insults the original.
annotation.definitionFit: A travesty is a grotesque imitation of something serious, which makes a mockery of it rather than merely copying it.

entries.clue: Wine professionals picked up reverberation (8)

indicatorNotes.picked up: Something picked up is something heard, so the word beside it is to be taken by its sound and written out that way.

blocks.note: pros is the everyday short form for professionals
a reverberation is an echo, and that sound written out with a hard double c gives the four letters needed

annotation.surface: Wine experts catch the sound of an echo.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Wine professionals' reads as one job — sommeliers — and only the first word is the definition. The back half is spelt by ear, which is why the letters look Italian.
annotation.definitionFit: Prosecco is the dry sparkling white from the Veneto, a wine on the plainest reading of the word.

entries.clue: A number observed around incident (9)

indicatorNotes.around: Putting one word around another wraps it, so the first piece opens up and closes again on both sides of the second.

blocks.note: observed is seen, and the four letters split one and three to make room
an incident is an event, five letters dropped into the gap

annotation.surface: A crowd of onlookers stood round the scene of an incident.
annotation.walkthrough: 'A number' stays deliberately vague and could be any of a hundred answers until a crossing letter or two arrives. The outer word breaks after a single letter, which is the hard part to see.
annotation.definitionFit: Seventeen is a number, and the definition names the class rather than the value — the grid settles which one.

entries.clue: Ragtime in China? (3,3)

annotation.definitionNote: China is the material and the crockery made from it; the question mark concedes that the answer is one thing made of china rather than a synonym for it.

blocks.note: the rag at the front of the word means to tease, the British sense of ragging someone
the time closing the word is t, the standard abbreviation for it

annotation.surface: Ragtime music is playing somewhere in China.
annotation.walkthrough: The one word 'Ragtime' has to be broken in two: ragging is British slang for teasing, and the second half is the physicist's letter for time. China is the crockery cupboard, not the country.
annotation.definitionFit: A tea set is the pot, cups and saucers, the classic household thing made of china, so the material stands for the object.

entries.clue: There’s a hip joint near here where The King is on piano (6)

annotation.definition: There’s a hip joint near here
annotation.definitionNote: The definition describes the place rather than naming the thing: it tells you where you are standing in the body, and the answer is the bone the hip joint is set into.

indicatorNotes.on: In an across entry a thing said to be on another is written after it, so the singer's letters follow the one for the instrument.

blocks.note: p is the marking on a score for piano, meaning played softly
Elvis Presley is the King of rock and roll, the title used on its own

annotation.surface: There is a fashionable club nearby where Elvis plays the piano.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Hip joint' does duty twice: the trendy bar the surface wants, and the ball-and-socket of anatomy. The single letter is the quiet marking on sheet music rather than the instrument itself.
annotation.definitionFit: The pelvis is the basin of bone at the base of the spine, with a socket on each side that the hip joint turns in.

entries.clue: Describe former unit of currency (7)

blocks.note: an ex is a former partner, and ex- is the prefix for former
the pound is Britain's unit of currency

annotation.surface: An account of some currency unit that is no longer in use.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface offers 'former unit of currency' as one phrase, some abandoned coin, and the clue wants those two ideas read apart. Expounding is setting a thing out at length rather than mentioning it.
annotation.definitionFit: To expound something is to set it out fully in words, which is describing it in detail.

entries.clue: Boisterous chaps taking home vegetable (7)

indicatorNotes.Boisterous: A boisterous crowd will not stay where it is put, and letters in that state come out in some other order.

blocks.note: five letters for the pile, taken for their spelling and not the men
someone at home is in, so two more letters join the pile

annotation.surface: Rowdy blokes bring a vegetable back to the house.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Home' is the crossword's two-letter word for in, and here those letters join the shuffle rather than telling you to put something inside something else. Seven letters go into the pile and seven come out.
annotation.definitionFit: Spinach is the dark leafy green sold in bunches or bags, a vegetable in the plainest sense.

entries.clue: Milk producer Ian is after chips (8)

indicatorNotes.after: What comes after something follows it, so the man's name is written behind the letters for the food.

blocks.note: chips are fries on an American menu, the same fried potatoes either way
the man's name goes in whole, letter for letter

annotation.surface: Ian joins the queue behind the chips at the counter.
annotation.walkthrough: The milk producer is a cow rather than a dairy or a farmer: the Friesian is the black-and-white breed that fills most British milk tankers. Chips and fries are the British and American words for one thing.
annotation.definitionFit: A Friesian is the black-and-white dairy breed, so the milk producer is the animal itself.

entries.clue: Pals ignoring first of rebellious devils (6)

indicatorNotes.ignoring: To ignore a letter is to leave it out altogether, so the longer word is written without the one named after it.

blocks.note: pals are friends, seven letters about to lose one
the opening letter of rebellious is R — that is the letter that goes

annotation.surface: Friends are leaving out the ringleader of a rebellious crowd.
annotation.walkthrough: The dropped letter is the second one, which is why the word survives the loss so neatly. 'Rebellious' is there only to be beheaded, not for its meaning.
annotation.definitionFit: A fiend is a devil or demon, the word used both for the literal one and for anyone behaving like it.

entries.clue: Free of inner hell (7)

indicatorNotes.Free: Something free is not held in place, so the letters beside it are loose and can be re-laid in any order.

blocks.note: seven letters for the pile, with 'of' counted as fodder rather than as joinery

annotation.surface: Someone has been released from a private hell.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Free of' looks like one phrase meaning rid of, and the clue splits it: the first word instructs and the second joins the pile. That is how the count reaches seven.
annotation.definitionFit: An inferno is hell itself — Dante's name for it — and by extension any fire fierce enough to deserve the comparison.

entries.clue: Opposed to Oscar being supported by church in ancient city (7)

indicatorNotes.supported by: In a down entry whatever supports something else sits underneath it, so the church's letters go below the ones they prop up.

blocks.note: anti means opposed to, the word taken whole
Oscar is the radio alphabet's word for the letter O
ch is the standard abbreviation for church, as printed on maps

annotation.surface: An opponent of Oscar's has the backing of the church in an old city.
annotation.walkthrough: Oscar is the letter O in the radio alphabet a coastguard uses, not a person, and the surface leans on the name to hide that. Antioch was the great Greek and Roman city in Syria, now Antakya in southern Turkey.
annotation.definitionFit: Antioch was one of the largest cities of the ancient world, founded after Alexander and later a centre of early Christianity.

entries.clue: Start to attack feature of some old front rooms (4,4)

annotation.definition2: feature of some old front rooms

blocks.note: the order shouted to soldiers, telling them to begin shooting

blocks.clueFragment: feature of some old front rooms
blocks.note: the coal or log fire burning in a parlour grate, the other reading of the same two words

annotation.surface: Someone begins an assault on something found in old parlours.
annotation.walkthrough: In British houses the front room is the parlour kept for visitors, and the feature in it is the hearth. Said to soldiers, the same two words are an order to start shooting.
annotation.definitionFit: To open fire is to begin shooting, and an open fire is the grate burning in a hearth — the same two words for the attack and for the fireplace.

entries.clue: Stuff in itemised boxes limited in nature (6)

indicatorNotes.boxes: To box something is to shut it in, so the words in front hold the answer unbroken inside them.

blocks.note: the run starts on the second f of stuff and carries straight through 'in' and into itemised

annotation.surface: Belongings are packed into labelled boxes.
annotation.walkthrough: The hiding place crosses two word breaks and starts halfway through a doubled letter, which is what keeps it out of sight. 'In nature' belongs to the definition, not to the hiding place.
annotation.definitionFit: Something finite has bounds — a finite number, a finite supply — so by its very nature it is limited.

entries.clue: Drunk announcement of relative’s specialism (5)

indicatorNotes.Drunk announcement of: An announcement is made aloud, and a drunk one comes out slurred, so the word after it is taken by a thickened version of its sound.

blocks.note: a relative is a niece, and slurred by a drunk those letters land on a different spelling

annotation.surface: A drunk is announcing what a relative of his is good at.
annotation.walkthrough: The joke is the slur: sober it is a family member, drunk it is the little corner of a market a business makes its own. Drunkenness as a homophone signal is rarer than the usual 'we hear'.
annotation.definitionFit: A specialism is the narrow field someone has made their own, which is exactly the corner of a market or a subject the word describes.

entries.clue: For certain, ruled out one working in the dead centre? (7,8)

annotation.definition: one working in the dead centre

indicatorNotes.out: Something out is out of its proper order, so the letters in front are tipped over and laid down again differently.

blocks.note: fifteen letters for the pile, the comma punctuation for the surface only

annotation.surface: Somebody has certainly been ruled out of a job right at the middle of things.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Ruled out' reads as one phrase meaning eliminated, and only its second word is the instruction — the first joins the pile. 'Dead centre' is the bullseye in the surface and the chapel of rest in the answer.
annotation.definitionFit: A funeral director's work is entirely among the dead, so 'the dead centre' reads as the premises rather than the exact middle of anything.

entries.clue: Hard to enter dark and depressing boat (6)

indicatorNotes.to enter: A letter told to enter a word goes inside it rather than beside it, breaking the word open to make room.

blocks.note: a dingy room is dark, drab and cheerless — one adjective for the whole phrase
H is the pencil grade meaning hard, the standard shorthand

annotation.surface: It is hard to climb into a dark and cheerless little boat.
annotation.walkthrough: Pencil grades are a crossword staple — H for hard, B for black, F for fine — and one of them supplies the letter going in. 'Dark and depressing' is four words for a single adjective, not two separate pieces.
annotation.definitionFit: A dinghy is a small open boat, the kind rowed out to a moored yacht or sailed for sport.

entries.clue: Record boring joke for credulous husband? (6)

annotation.definitionNote: The answer is a name, and the definition points at one particular holder of it — Mary's husband in the nativity story, who took her account on trust — which is what the question mark admits.

indicatorNotes.boring: Boring is the drilling verb here, so the piece beside it is driven into the middle of the other one.

blocks.note: to josh someone is to joke with them, and the word opens before its last letter
an EP is an extended-play record, longer than a single and shorter than an album

annotation.surface: A dull record has become a standing joke with some gullible husband.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Boring' is the verb for drilling rather than the adjective for dull, which is the one swap the whole clue turns on. The husband is the one from the nativity, believing what he was told.
annotation.definitionFit: Joseph accepted Mary's explanation of her pregnancy, which is the joke behind calling him a credulous husband.
